cues.text: Q11 Emergency. Quantum Emergency Response: a toy city where fires are quantum errors, alarm stations are parity checks, and you are the dispatcher.
Your first call takes three taps. Pick a crew, tap the house, and spray.
Both alarms ring, so the fire must be in the house they both watch.
Answer check. The truck arrives, the crew runs in, and one hose is exactly one Pauli correction.
Fires out, houses restored. X times X is the identity.
This is the city map. Districts unlock in order, the smoke clears, and you earn a badge.
Dispatch! The fire truck drives to Harbor Bridge.
Training first. Tap where the fire will be after the gate. A red fire copies forward through the coupler.
And a blue fire copies backward.
Now the challenge. A red fire starts on house zero and a blue fire on house one. After the gate, both houses carry a red-and-blue fire, so we send a Y crew to each.
Watch the fires travel first. Through the coupler the red fire copies forward and the blue fire copies backward. Then the crews spray, and every pair cancels.
For reviewers there is free selection: with this switch every district opens from the map.
Central District is the distance-three surface code. Nine houses, eight alarm stations.
Here the fires are hidden behind fog. Tap a station to see which houses it watches.
Z zero and Z one both ring, and only house four is watched by both. So we plan a red crew there and spray.
The hose reveals the true fire, puts it out, and every station goes quiet.
Central District is restored and a new badge is earned. With free selection, Old Town is already open.
Old Town. One alarm rings, and the best explanation is a single fire on house zero.
Every alarm goes quiet. And yet the memory tower flips. Two fires fooled the alarms. That is what distance three means.
Why? Your spray and the alternative, side by side. The investigation is complete: nobody could have known from the alarms alone.
The same missions run as Qiskit circuits on Qollab. Exact on the built-in simulator, and on IonQ's Aria 1 simulator the logical bit flipped in ninety-seven percent of shots.
